In this study, we investigate the size effect on the deformation behaviour of nanocrystalline (nc) bcc Fe. We employed micro-compression tests of single pillars with diameters ranging from 500 nm to 5 \(\mu\)m. We observe a pronounced size effect on the deformation behaviour of nc Fe. The m-values decrease with decreasing pillar diameter and are in the range of 1/20.001-0.02. This is in contrast to the expectations from classical dislocation theories [7,8] and even to the results on nc fcc metals [9]. We discuss possible explanations for this discrepancy and present a model for the size effect on the deformation behaviour of nc bcc metals.

As a result, the end product of digital photography is a perfect copy, thus eliminating the possibility of an "original" art object. This is an important distinction for our purposes. The digital process creates an art object (the original digital file) that can be copied infinitely without losing any data. The resulting objects (the copies) are perfect replicas of the original. In contrast, traditional art objects (e.g., paintings, sculptures, etc.) cannot be copied with such precision and fidelity. In this sense, the digital photograph has "changed" the nature of the "photograph" as a medium.

This is a critical point of difference between analog and digital photography - the former requires one to create a new print every time the original is desired; the latter allows one to copy the original file (or a derivative) with complete fidelity. This is not to say that digital photographs are without limitations. As with any technology, there are trade-offs that must be considered. Digital images are often limited by the file size and resolution of the capture device (camera) and the image-editing software. For example, an image taken with a high-end camera might have a file size of 20 megabytes, making it difficult to transmit over the Internet or store on a digital device (e.g., smartphone). The resolution of the image is also important, as it determines the level of detail and sharpness that can be achieved in the final image. Furthermore, the software used to edit the image can introduce additional limitations, such as the availability of specific filters or the ability to adjust certain aspects of the image.

As an example, consider a hospital that has a budget constraint for surgical procedures. This is a critical point of difference between analog and digital photography - the former requires one to create a new print every time the original art object is reproduced, while the latter allows for perfect replication (or near-perfect replication, in the case of lossy compression) of the original. The digital photograph, as an art form, offers a unique challenge to the artist in that it requires one to consider the ways in which the digital file can be manipulated and manipulated in a way that is faithful to the original aesthetic intent of the work. The digital photograph is not simply a reproduction of an analog original, but rather a new and unique expression of the artist's vision. It is in this way that digital photography can be seen as a distinct art form in its own right, one that challenges and pushes the boundaries of traditional notions of what constitutes a photograph.

This is a major paradigm shift for any artist who has to deal with the variable nature of any analog media.
In terms of the art object, the photograph is not a photograph until it is printed. What you see on the back of your camera is merely a preview of what the photograph will look like once it is printed. Thus, the final art object is the print, and because it is a digital file, it can be printed on any number of surfaces - paper, canvas, aluminum, wood, etc. The nature of the art object is quite different from the traditional photograph and is one of the most exciting aspects of digital photography for artists. The other interesting aspect is that you can create digital images that are not photographs at all. For example, you can combine photos taken with your camera with other graphics and then print the results on a variety of surfaces. The fact that you can manipulate digital files in any number of ways to create a final product is both exciting and liberating for artists.

In this paper, we present an EMG pattern recognition system for controlling a wrist prosthesis. The system consists of a pattern recognition module and a classifier. The pattern recognition module is used to extract movement-related information from the EMG signals and the classifier is used to classify the extracted features into a corresponding prosthesis function. The pattern recognition module and the classifier are trained and tested, respectively, on a dataset from able-bodied individuals. The EMG signals are recorded from six different locations of the forearm (Fig. 1). In order to reduce the dimensionality of the feature space, while retaining the salient information, we use the singular value decomposition (SVD) and the linear discriminant analysis (LDA) feature extraction methods. To classify the extracted features, we employ the linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and the support vector machine (SVM) classifiers.

It is a key determinant of the ways in which social learning takes place in a society (Henrich, 2004; Henrich et al., 2001, 2010; Richerson & Boyd, 2005). Here, we present an overview of the current AI developments within the field of aging research, with a focus on the following aspects: (1) the use of AI to analyze and classify the data generated by high-throughput experiments and (2) the use of AI to generate novel hypotheses, to predict novel aging-related genes and to identify novel aging-related pathways. We also highlight the current challenges and future perspectives of AI in the field of aging research. Finally, we outline the major AI challenges within the field of aging research, including the need for the development of new open source tools and for the improvement of data quality.

Therefore, this paper presents a decision rule for optimal resource allocation in settings with persistent constraints.
The purpose of this paper is to show that the decision rule for optimal resource allocation is dependent on the presence of constraints. In particular, we show that when one or more of the constraints are binding, the decision rule for optimal resource allocation depends on the relative strengths of the constraints. We do this by presenting a new decision rule, which we call the relative strength decision rule. This decision rule takes into account the relative strengths of the constraints and the constraints that are binding, when making resource allocation decisions. We further show how the relative strength decision rule can be applied in the context of the Norwegian health care system.
The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the basic model and the derivation of the relative strength decision rule. Section 3 discusses the application of the relative strength decision rule to the Norwegian health care system. Section 4 presents a summary of the paper and the conclusions.

We investigate how the cultural organization of society shapes the selection of social learning strategies in two ways. First, we manipulate the size of the social learning group, and we demonstrate that social learning strategies are more often selected when the group size is large rather than small. In this paper, we present an alternative approach that enables amputees to use EMG-based pattern recognition for prosthesis control without the need for extensive training. Our approach uses a novel method for mapping EMG signals to prostheses functions. The method does not require explicit classification of EMG signals. Instead, it uses a "voting" mechanism to decide which prostheses function to execute. We demonstrate that our approach can be implemented on a hand prosthesis without the need for explicit training. In our experiments, we also demonstrate that our approach can be implemented on a wrist prosthesis without the need for explicit training. In addition, we demonstrate that our approach is robust to variations in EMG signals, which are often observed in amputees.

For example, one can take a photograph of the Grand Canyon and remove the sky, change the color, change the size, add text, etc. and create an entirely new photograph. The image is no longer a static object but a dynamic one where one can alter the original image in any number of ways. This is what makes digital photography so exciting for artists. It is a key determinant of the ways in which people cooperate or compete with each other (Greif, 2006; Henrich et al., 2001, 2010; Santos et al., 2011). Our main finding is that social learning strategies are shaped by the cultural organization of a society. The experiment was conducted in the form of a public goods game, a classic experimental paradigm where individual contributions to a public good are multiplied by a factor \(r\), where \(r\) is the level of contribution of others in the group. The higher the \(r\), the greater the benefit of cooperation. We find that individuals conform to local majorities and that this conformity effect is stronger for larger groups. We also show that this effect is independent of the decision context (i.e., whether the game is played within a group or across groups), the strength of the local majority, and the level of cooperation required by the local majority. The results suggest that a conformist strategy of social learning can be robustly observed in a laboratory setting, but the implications for the evolution of cooperation are mixed.
